particleNote.explanation: Marks the direct object. Whatever is being eaten takes 'を'.
particleNote.example: 湯豆腐を食べる。(I eat yudofu.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 Why the Te-form (食べて) is crucial
grammarNote.content: The Te-form acts as the 'glue' of Japanese sentences. You can't just say 'I eat. I go.' You use the Te-form to connect them: 朝ごはんを食べて、学校に行きます (I eat breakfast, AND THEN I go to school).

particleNote.explanation: Marks the direct object — what is being drunk takes 'を'.
particleNote.example: コーヒーを飲む。(I drink coffee.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 Te-form of む-ending verbs
grammarNote.content: Godan verbs ending in む change to んで in the Te-form: 飲む → 飲んで. This sound change (音便 / おんびん) applies to ぬ and ぶ endings too. Example: コーヒーを飲んで、元気になりました (I drank coffee and felt better).

particleNote.explanation: Marks the destination. 'に' focuses on the arrival point, 'へ' on the direction.
particleNote.example: 箱根に行く。(I go to Hakone.)

grammarNote.title: ⚠️ The one irregular Te-form in Godan verbs
grammarNote.content: 行く is the ONLY Godan く-verb whose Te-form is いって (not いいて). All other く-verbs follow the rule: 書く → 書いて. Remember: 行って is an exception. It pairs with に or へ: 学校に行って、勉強します (I go to school and study).

particleNote.explanation: Marks where someone comes to. Movement is toward the speaker.
particleNote.example: 日本に来る。(I come to Japan.)

grammarNote.title: ⚠️ 来る is one of only two irregular verbs
grammarNote.content: Japanese has just two truly irregular verbs: する and 来る. All forms of 来る change the root: く → き → こ. Watch for: 来て (kite), 来ない (konai), 来た (kita). Direction matters: use 来る when movement is toward the speaker, 行く when away.

particleNote.explanation: Marks the activity or noun being done. Many nouns + を + する become verbs.
particleNote.example: 宿題をする。(I do homework.)

grammarNote.title: ⚠️ する turns nouns into verbs
grammarNote.content: する is the most productive verb in Japanese. Add it after almost any noun to mean 'to do [noun]': 勉強する (study), 運動する (exercise), 電話する (phone). For N5 exams, memorise: します (polite), して (Te-form), しない (negative), した (past).

meaning: to see / to watch / to look at

particleNote.explanation: Marks what is watched or looked at.
particleNote.example: 映画を見る。(I watch a movie.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 見る vs 見える — 'to watch' vs 'to be visible'
grammarNote.content: 見る is an intentional action: テレビを見る (watch TV). 見える is potential/involuntary: 富士山が見える (Mt Fuji can be seen). For N5, focus on 見る. Common pattern: 〜てみる = try doing something: 食べてみる (try eating it).

meaning: to listen / to hear / to ask

particleNote.explanation: 'を' for what you listen to; 'に' for the person you ask.
particleNote.example: 音楽を聞く。(I listen to music.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 聞く has three meanings — context decides
grammarNote.content: 聞く can mean listen (音楽を聞く), hear (音が聞こえる is different), or ask (先生に聞く). For N5 exams, the particle signals the meaning: を for listening, に for asking. Te-form: く → いて, so 聞いて.

particleNote.explanation: 'と' for the person you talk with; 'で' for the language used.
particleNote.example: 日本語で話す。(I speak in Japanese.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 The す → して Te-form rule
grammarNote.content: Godan verbs ending in す always form their Te-form with して: 話す → 話して, 貸す → 貸して, 押す → 押して. There are no exceptions to this rule. Example: 日本語で話してください (Please speak in Japanese).

particleNote.explanation: Marks what is written.
particleNote.example: 手紙を書く。(I write a letter.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 く → いて: the standard Te-form rule for く-verbs
grammarNote.content: Most く-ending Godan verbs change to いて: 書く → 書いて, 歩く → 歩いて, 聞く → 聞いて. The only exception is 行く → 行って. Remember this rule and the one exception, and you've covered almost all く-verbs at N5.

particleNote.explanation: Marks what is read.
particleNote.example: 本を読む。(I read a book.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 む → んで: the nasal sound change
grammarNote.content: む-ending Godan verbs use the 'nasal Te-form' — む → んで: 読む → 読んで. This follows the same pattern as 飲む → 飲んで and 休む → 休んで. In N5 reading passages, 〜を読んでいます (am reading ~) appears very frequently.

meaning: to wake up / to get up

particleNote.explanation: No direct object. The subject (you) wakes up by itself; time takes に.
particleNote.example: 七時に起きる。(I wake up at 7.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 起きる vs 起こす — intransitive vs transitive
grammarNote.content: 起きる = wake up by yourself (intransitive). 起こす = wake someone else up (transitive). This pair is a classic N5 trap. Example: 毎朝7時に起きます (I wake up at 7 every morning). 子どもを起こします (I wake the child up).

meaning: to sleep / to go to bed

particleNote.explanation: No direct object. Time of sleeping takes に.
particleNote.example: 十一時に寝る。(I go to bed at 11.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 Time expressions with 寝る
grammarNote.content: 寝る commonly pairs with time words and the まえに (before) or てから (after) patterns. 寝るまえに歯を磨きます (I brush my teeth before sleeping). 〜時間寝ます (sleep for ~ hours). These sentence structures appear regularly in N5 reading.

particleNote.explanation: Marks what is bought.
particleNote.example: 新しい服を買う。(I buy new clothes.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 う-ending Godan verbs: the hidden わ row
grammarNote.content: Verbs ending in う look like they should use the あ sound in the Nai-form — but う-final Godan verbs use わ instead: 買う → 買わない (not 買あない). This applies to 言う、使う、洗う、会う too. Te-form: 買う → 買って (う → って).

particleNote.explanation: Marks the tool or object used.
particleNote.example: パソコンを使う。(I use a computer.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 使う takes を for the thing used
grammarNote.content: The thing being used always takes を: パソコンを使います (I use a computer). Confusingly, 使う sometimes competes with する in meaning — but 使う focuses on a tool or object. N5 tip: 〜を使って (using ~) is a very common connective pattern.

particleNote.explanation: Marks the person you meet — NOT を.
particleNote.example: 友だちに会う。(I meet a friend.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 会う takes に, not を
grammarNote.content: Unlike English 'meet someone', 会う uses に for the person met: 友だちに会います (I meet a friend). Using を here is a common mistake. Contrast: 見る takes を. In N5 reading passages, 〜に会いに行く (go to meet ~) is a very common structure.

particleNote.explanation: Marks what or who is waited for.
particleNote.example: バスを待つ。(I wait for the bus.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 つ → って: the small っ (double consonant) rule
grammarNote.content: Godan verbs ending in つ use って for the Te-form: 待つ → 待って, 立つ → 立って, 持つ → 持って. The same double-consonant pattern applies to う and る Godan verbs too: 買う → 買って, 帰る → 帰って. Station PA systems love 〜をお待ちください.

meaning: to hold / to carry / to have

particleNote.explanation: Marks what is held or carried.
particleNote.example: かばんを持つ。(I carry a bag.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 持つ vs 持っている — momentary vs ongoing
grammarNote.content: 持つ is the action of picking up / holding. 持っている describes a continuing state: something you carry or own. カバンを持っています (I have/am carrying a bag). This 〜ている pattern for ongoing states is tested frequently in N5 grammar.

particleNote.explanation: Place returned to takes に/へ; place left takes を.
particleNote.example: 家に帰る。(I return home.)

grammarNote.title: ⚠️ 帰る is a Godan verb — don't be tricked!
grammarNote.content: 帰る ends in る but it's Godan, not Ichidan. The Te-form is 帰って (not 帰て). Other common Godan る-verbs at N5: 走る、切る、知る、入る、帰る. A reliable sign: if the vowel before る is a, u, or o — it's almost always Godan.

particleNote.explanation: Marks what you enter into.
particleNote.example: 部屋に入る。(I enter the room.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 入る (Godan) vs 入れる (Ichidan)
grammarNote.content: 入る (はいる) = to enter (intransitive — you go in): 部屋に入ります. 入れる (いれる) = to put in / insert (transitive): コインを入れます. N5 exams test this transitive/intransitive pair. Remember: 入る is Godan → Te-form 入って.

meaning: to go out / to leave / to appear

particleNote.explanation: Marks the place you exit from.
particleNote.example: 家を出る。(I leave the house.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 出る is the opposite of 入る
grammarNote.content: 出る (でる) = to come/go out: 家を出ます (I leave the house). Note it takes を, not に/から. Its transitive partner is 出す (to take out / to hand in): しゅくだいを出す (hand in homework). 出る also means 'to appear/be served': 料理が出ます.

particleNote.explanation: Marks the vehicle you board — NOT を.
particleNote.example: 電車に乗る。(I get on the train.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 乗る takes に for the vehicle
grammarNote.content: The vehicle you board takes に: 電車に乗ります (ride the train). Contrast with 乗り換える (のりかえる = transfer / change trains). The opposite is 降りる (おりる = to get off). These transport verbs are staples of N5 schedule and route questions.

particleNote.explanation: Place of getting off takes で; vehicle exited takes を.
particleNote.example: 次の駅で降りる。(I get off at the next station.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 Always paired with 乗る in transport contexts
grammarNote.content: 乗る (get on) and 降りる (get off) always appear together in N5 travel scenarios. 次の駅で降ります (I get off at the next station). Takes で for the stop: 東京駅で降ります. Don't confuse 降りる (get off) with 下がる (go down in value/level).

particleNote.explanation: No object. Destination takes まで/に.
particleNote.example: 駅まで歩く。(I walk to the station.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 歩いて = 'on foot' — a fixed expression
grammarNote.content: 歩いて (the Te-form used adverbially) means 'on foot': 駅まで歩いていきます (I go to the station on foot). This pattern — Te-form + 行く/来る — means 'go/come doing [action]' and is common in N5 travel and schedule passages. 徒歩(とほ) is the formal written equivalent.

particleNote.explanation: No object. Place run takes を (path) or で.
particleNote.example: 公園を走る。(I run in the park.)

grammarNote.title: ⚠️ 走る is Godan despite looking like Ichidan
grammarNote.content: 走る ends in iru but is Godan: 走ります (polite), 走って (Te-form), 走らない (Nai). If it were Ichidan it would be 走ります → 走りて, which doesn't exist. Test yourself: if 〜ない ends in らない it's Godan; if it ends in ない with no ら it's Ichidan.

particleNote.explanation: No object. Place swum takes で.
particleNote.example: 海で泳ぐ。(I swim in the sea.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 ぐ → いで: the voiced Te-form rule
grammarNote.content: Godan verbs ending in ぐ change to いで in the Te-form: 泳ぐ → 泳いで, 急ぐ → 急いで. This is the voiced equivalent of く → いて. Remember: ぐ and く both become い + consonant, but ぐ stays voiced as で not て.

meaning: to play / to have fun / to hang out

particleNote.explanation: No object. Place played takes で.
particleNote.example: 公園で遊ぶ。(I play in the park.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 ぶ → んで: voiced nasal Te-form
grammarNote.content: Godan verbs ending in ぶ form the Te-form with んで: 遊ぶ → 遊んで, 呼ぶ → 呼んで, 飛ぶ → 飛んで. Same sound change as む → んで. A nice N5 sentence: 公園で遊んでいます (playing at the park) — combine with 〜ている for ongoing action.

particleNote.explanation: Place of work takes で.
particleNote.example: 会社で働く。(I work at a company.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 働く vs する for 'work'
grammarNote.content: 働く focuses on the act of working (often physically or at a job): 会社で働きます (I work at a company). 仕事をする is a synonymous phrase using する. Working location takes で. Common N5 reading context: 〜で働いている (currently working at ~) using 〜ている for ongoing state.

meaning: to rest / to take a day off / to be absent

particleNote.explanation: What you are absent from / rest takes を.
particleNote.example: 学校を休む。(I'm absent from school.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 休む covers rest, absence, and breaks
grammarNote.content: 休む is versatile: 今日は学校を休みます (I'm absent from school today), 昼休みに休みます (I rest during lunch break), 土曜日は休みます (I take Saturday off). The noun 休み (やすみ) = day off / holiday. N5 tip: 〜をやすむ = be absent from ~, taking を.

particleNote.explanation: Marks the subject studied.
particleNote.example: 日本語を勉強する。(I study Japanese.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 Suru-compound verbs follow する's conjugation
grammarNote.content: 勉強する = 勉強 (study, noun) + する. All suru-compound verbs conjugate exactly like する: 勉強します、勉強して、勉強しない、勉強した. You can also separate the noun: 勉強をします. Both forms are correct. N5 exams test whether you know these compounds are verbs, not just nouns.

conjugations.japanese: 勉強しないでください
勉強する でしょう

particleNote.explanation: Marks what is practised.
particleNote.example: ピアノを練習する。(I practise the piano.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 練習 is common in N5 hobby and club passages
grammarNote.content: 練習する appears in passages about sports clubs, music lessons, and language study. まいにち練習しています (I practise every day) is a textbook N5 sentence combining 〜ている for habitual action. The noun 練習 (れんしゅう) also appears in N5 vocabulary sections.

conjugations.japanese: 練習しないでください
練習する でしょう

meaning: to teach / to tell / to inform

particleNote.explanation: に marks the person taught; を marks what is taught.
particleNote.example: 学生に日本語を教える。(I teach students Japanese.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 教える takes two objects: に and を
grammarNote.content: Like English 'teach someone something', 教える uses に for the person and を for what is taught: 田中さんに日本語を教えます (I teach Tanaka Japanese). This double-object structure also appears with あげる/もらう verbs and is a core N5 grammar pattern.

meaning: to learn (from a teacher) / to take lessons

particleNote.explanation: を marks what is learned; に/から marks the teacher.
particleNote.example: 先生にピアノを習う。(I learn piano from a teacher.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 習う vs 勉強する vs 覚える
grammarNote.content: 習う = learn through instruction/lessons (から or に marks the teacher: 先生に習う). 勉強する = study (self-directed or general). 覚える = memorise / learn by heart. N5 exams test which is natural in context. 日本語を習っています (I'm taking Japanese lessons) implies a teacher.

meaning: to understand / to know / to be clear

particleNote.explanation: Marks what is understood — NOT を.
particleNote.example: 日本語が分かる。(I understand Japanese.)

grammarNote.title: ⚠️ 分かる uses が, not を — a classic N5 particle trap
grammarNote.content: Unlike English 'I understand Japanese', 分かる takes が: 日本語が分かります (Japanese is understandable to me). Using を here is one of the most common N5 errors. Similarly: 名前が分かりません (I don't know the name). 分かりました is also the standard 'I understand / Got it.'

conjugations.japanese: 分からないでください

meaning: to come to know / to find out

particleNote.explanation: Marks what becomes known.
particleNote.example: 彼の名前を知る。(I find out his name.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 知っている = 'to know' (the state of knowing)
grammarNote.content: 知る means the act of coming to know. The ongoing state — 'to know (something)' — is always expressed as 知っている: 田中さんを知っています (I know Tanaka). Saying 田中さんを知ります is unnatural. Negative: 知りません or 知らない. This 〜ている for states is a critical N5 distinction.

meaning: to think / to feel / to believe

particleNote.explanation: Marks the quoted thought (plain form + と).
particleNote.example: 明日は雨だと思う。(I think it'll rain tomorrow.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 〜と思います: quoting your own opinion
grammarNote.content: 思う is almost always preceded by the quotation particle と: 明日は雨だと思います (I think it will rain tomorrow). The clause before と must end in plain form. This pattern appears in nearly every N5 grammar section. Compare with 〜と言います (says that ~), which uses the same structure.

particleNote.explanation: Marks the quoted speech (plain form + と).
particleNote.example: 「行く」と言う。(He says 'I'll go.')

grammarNote.title: 💡 〜と言います: quoting what someone says
grammarNote.content: 言う almost always pairs with the quotation particle と: 「行きます」と言いました (said 'I'll go'). Also used for names: これは日本語で何と言いますか (What do you say this in Japanese?). Te-form 言って enables: 言ってください (please say it), 言っています (is saying).

particleNote.explanation: Marks what you open — transitive.
particleNote.example: 窓を開ける。(I open the window.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 開ける (transitive) vs 開く (intransitive)
grammarNote.content: 開ける = you open it (takes を): 窓を開けます (I open the window). 開く = it opens by itself (no を): ドアが開きます (the door opens). This transitive/intransitive pair is a classic N5 exam topic. Related: 閉める/閉まる (close) follows the exact same pattern.

particleNote.explanation: Marks what you close — transitive.
particleNote.example: ドアを閉める。(I close the door.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 閉める (transitive) vs 閉まる (intransitive)
grammarNote.content: 閉める = you close it: ドアを閉めてください (please close the door). 閉まる = it closes: ドアが閉まります (the door closes). Shops also use 閉まる: 店が閉まっています (the shop is closed). These ある/える intransitive/transitive pairs are tested heavily in N5.

meaning: to turn on / to attach / to apply

particleNote.explanation: Marks what is turned on / attached.
particleNote.example: 電気をつける。(I turn on the light.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 つける/けす — turning appliances on and off
grammarNote.content: つける = turn on (lights, TV, etc.): 電気をつけます. けす (消す) = turn off: 電気を消します. Both are essential for N5 sign-reading and comprehension passages. Note: けす is a Godan verb (消す → 消して). These are among the most useful verbs for daily life in Japan.

meaning: to turn off / to erase / to extinguish

particleNote.explanation: Marks what is turned off / erased.
particleNote.example: テレビを消す。(I turn off the TV.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 消す is the opposite of つける in most contexts
grammarNote.content: 電気を消す (turn off the light), テレビを消す (turn off the TV), 黒板を消す (erase the board). The す → して rule applies: 消して = Te-form. At N5, ～を消してください (please turn off ~) appears in instructions and daily-life dialogues.

particleNote.explanation: Marks what is washed.
particleNote.example: 手を洗う。(I wash my hands.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 洗う in daily routine sentences
grammarNote.content: 洗う appears in routine descriptions: 顔を洗います (wash my face), 手を洗います (wash my hands), 皿を洗います (wash the dishes). The N5 pattern 〜を洗ってから (after washing ~) uses 洗う's Te-form. Signs like 手を洗ってください are common in N5 sign-reading questions.

particleNote.explanation: Marks the upper-body clothing worn.
particleNote.example: シャツを着る。(I wear a shirt.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 Wearing verbs in Japanese are body-part-specific
grammarNote.content: Japanese has different 'wear' verbs depending on what body part: 着る (shirts, jackets — torso), はく (pants, shoes, socks — waist down), かぶる (hats — head), する or つける (accessories — watch, glasses). N5 exams test this distinction. All take を.

particleNote.explanation: Marks any clothing removed.
particleNote.example: 靴を脱ぐ。(I take off my shoes.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 脱ぐ is the opposite of all the 'wear' verbs
grammarNote.content: While 着る/はく/かぶる all have different 'put on' verbs, 脱ぐ covers ALL clothing types when removing: シャツを脱ぐ (take off shirt), 靴を脱ぐ (take off shoes), 帽子を脱ぐ (take off hat). In Japan, 靴を脱いでください (please remove your shoes) is a very real instruction.

meaning: to make / to cook / to create

particleNote.explanation: Marks what is made or cooked.
particleNote.example: 料理を作る。(I cook a meal.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 作る for food, objects, and systems
grammarNote.content: 作る covers making almost anything: 料理を作る (cook a meal), 計画を作る (make a plan), 友だちを作る (make friends — an idiomatic use). Common in N5 hobby and daily-life passages. 〜を作っています (I am making ~) uses 〜ている for actions in progress.

particleNote.explanation: Marks what starts — intransitive.
particleNote.example: 授業が始まる。(Class starts.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 始まる (intransitive) vs 始める (transitive)
grammarNote.content: 始まる = something starts on its own: 授業が始まります (class starts). 始める = someone starts something: 日本語を始めます (I start Japanese). The subject of 始まる takes が; the object of 始める takes を. Both appear in N5 schedules and event descriptions.

conjugations.japanese: 始まらないでください

particleNote.explanation: Marks what ends — intransitive.
particleNote.example: 映画が終わる。(The film ends.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 終わる vs 終える — same distinction as 始まる/始める
grammarNote.content: 終わる = it ends by itself: 映画が終わります (the film ends). 終える = you finish it: 仕事を終えます (I finish my work). N5 schedule questions frequently ask about start and end times, making 始まる and 終わる two of the most practical verbs to master. 〜が終わったら (when ~ finishes) is a common connective.

conjugations.japanese: 終わらないでください

particleNote.explanation: に marks who you lend to; を marks what is lent.
particleNote.example: 友だちに本を貸す。(I lend a book to a friend.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 貸す vs 借りる — lend vs borrow
grammarNote.content: 貸す = lend (you give to someone): 本を貸します。借りる = borrow (you receive from someone): 本を借ります. The direction is from the speaker's perspective. N5 tip: 貸してください (please lend me ~) uses 貸す + Te-form + ください, a key request pattern.

particleNote.explanation: を marks what is borrowed; から marks the lender.
particleNote.example: 図書館から本を借りる。(I borrow a book from the library.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 借りる covers both borrow and rent
grammarNote.content: 借りる means borrow (temporarily use something from someone): 本を借りる (borrow a book), アパートを借りる (rent an apartment). The lender/owner takes から: 図書館から借りました (borrowed from the library). N5 passages about libraries frequently use 借りる.

particleNote.explanation: に marks the receiver; を marks the gift.
particleNote.example: 友だちにプレゼントをあげる。(I give my friend a present.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 The giving/receiving trio: あげる・もらう・くれる
grammarNote.content: This is one of N5's most tested grammar areas. あげる = I/we give (away from speaker): 友だちにプレゼントをあげます. もらう = I receive: 友だちにプレゼントをもらいます. くれる = someone gives TO me: 友だちがプレゼントをくれます. The verb choice encodes direction relative to the speaker.

particleNote.explanation: に/から marks the giver; を marks what's received.
particleNote.example: 友だちにプレゼントをもらう。(I receive a present from a friend.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 〜てもらう: 'have someone do something for you'
grammarNote.content: Beyond just 'receive', もらう combines with Te-forms to mean 'have ~ done for me': 先生に説明してもらいました (I had the teacher explain it). This is a fundamental N5 grammar structure expressing favours received. The benefactor takes に or から.

conjugations.japanese: もらわないでください

particleNote.explanation: が marks the giver (not you); を marks the gift.
particleNote.example: 母がケーキをくれる。(My mother gives me a cake.)

grammarNote.title: ⚠️ くれる always means someone gives TO me
grammarNote.content: The subject of くれる is always someone outside your in-group; the receiver is always you (or your family/close circle): 母がケーキをくれました (my mother gave me a cake). 〜てくれる means someone does something for you: 友だちが手伝ってくれました. If YOU are giving, use あげる, not くれる.

meaning: to put / to place / to leave (something somewhere)

particleNote.explanation: に marks where it's placed; を marks what is placed.
particleNote.example: 机の上に本を置く。(I put the book on the desk.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 〜ておく: do something in advance
grammarNote.content: 置く alone means to place: 机の上に置きます (I put it on the desk). But 〜ておく (Te-form + おく) is an N5 grammar point meaning 'do ~ in advance / do ~ and leave it that way': 予約しておきます (I'll book it in advance). Very common in practical, planning contexts.

particleNote.explanation: Marks what is forgotten.
particleNote.example: 宿題を忘れる。(I forget my homework.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 忘れる vs 忘れ物 — forgetting vs left-behind item
grammarNote.content: 忘れる is a common verb in N5 comprehension passages: 宿題を忘れました (forgot homework), 傘を忘れました (left umbrella behind). 忘れ物(わすれもの) = forgotten/lost item — useful for passages about finding lost items. 忘れないでください = please don't forget (〜ないでください = please don't ~).

meaning: to memorise / to learn / to remember

particleNote.explanation: Marks what is memorised.
particleNote.example: 単語を覚える。(I memorise vocabulary.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 覚える = actively commit to memory
grammarNote.content: 覚える is the active process of memorising: 単語を覚えます (memorise vocabulary). Its opposite is 忘れる. Don't confuse with 思い出す (おもいだす) = recall something you already knew. N5 study tip: 覚えておいてください (please memorise this) combines with 〜ておく for the 'do and keep' meaning.

group: Godan (U-verb) — same sound as 着る!

particleNote.explanation: Marks what is cut.
particleNote.example: 紙を切る。(I cut the paper.)

grammarNote.title: ⚠️ 切る (Godan) vs 着る (Ichidan) — homophone alert!
grammarNote.content: 切る (きる = cut) and 着る (きる = wear) sound identical but conjugate differently. 切る is Godan: 切ります、切って、切らない. 着る is Ichidan: 着ます、着て、着ない. Context and kanji tell them apart. N5 exams test this contrast. 〜を切る = cut ~, 〜を着る = wear ~.

particleNote.explanation: No object. Used alone or as a command.
particleNote.example: 急いでください。(Please hurry.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 急いで = 'hurry!' — Te-form used as a command
grammarNote.content: 急いでください (please hurry) and 急いで！(Hurry up!) are very common. The ぐ → いで Te-form rule: 急ぐ → 急いで. Also 急いでいます = I am in a hurry (ongoing state). N5 daily-life dialogues often include 急がなければなりません (I must hurry) — the must-do pattern.

particleNote.explanation: No object. Place stood takes に.
particleNote.example: ここに立つ。(I stand here.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 立つ vs 立っている — action vs state
grammarNote.content: 立つ = the action of standing up. 立っている = currently standing (state). This 〜ている distinction between action and resulting state is a core N5 grammar concept. 立ってください (please stand). Opposite: 座る (すわる = to sit down), which follows the same logic: 座っている = is sitting.

particleNote.explanation: Marks where you sit down.
particleNote.example: いすに座る。(I sit on the chair.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 座ってください — sit down please
grammarNote.content: 座ってください is one of the most common classroom and public-place instructions in Japanese. 座っています = is seated/sitting (state). A key N5 context: ここに座ってもいいですか (May I sit here?) — the 〜てもいいですか (may I ~?) permission-asking pattern with the Te-form.

meaning: to call (out to) / to invite / to summon

particleNote.explanation: Marks who/what is called or invited.
particleNote.example: タクシーを呼ぶ。(I call a taxi.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 呼ぶ for names, people, and invitations
grammarNote.content: 呼ぶ covers calling someone's name (名前で呼ぶ), calling/summoning (タクシーを呼ぶ — call a taxi), and inviting (パーティーに呼ぶ — invite to a party). ぶ → んで: 呼んで. よんでください = please call/invite. Don't confuse 呼ぶ (yobu = call) with 読む (yomu = read) — very similar sounds!

particleNote.explanation: Marks the task you help with.
particleNote.example: 料理を手伝う。(I help with the cooking.)

grammarNote.title: 💡 手伝う vs 助ける — two kinds of 'help'
grammarNote.content: 手伝う = help with a task (practical assistance): 料理を手伝います (help with cooking). 助ける (たすける) = rescue/save (from danger or difficulty). N5 passages about chores and daily life use 手伝う. 〜を手伝ってくれますか (will you help me with ~?) is a natural request structure combining 手伝う + Te-form + くれますか.

conjugations.japanese: 手伝わないでください
